report:
### Conclusion
The claim is **supported by scientific evidence**. Opening a bedroom door or window improves sleep quality for most people by enhancing ventilation and preventing carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) build-up overnight.

### Key Evidence
* **Reduced $\text{CO}_2$ Accumulation:** In sealed bedrooms, exhaled $\text{CO}_2$ often exceeds recommended thresholds ($>1,000\text{ ppm}$). Opening a door or window facilitates air exchange, keeping $\text{CO}_2$ levels low.
* **Better Sleep Quality:** Studies tracking sleepers using actigraphy and questionnaires show that enhanced ventilation lowers nighttime awakenings, increases sleep efficiency, and improves self-reported air freshness.
* **Cognitive Benefits:** Lower nighttime $\text{CO}_2$ levels are linked to reduced next-day sleepiness, improved concentration, and better cognitive test performance.

### Caveats
The strategy is beneficial provided it does not introduce negative environmental factors. If opening a window exposes the bedroom to excessive outdoor noise, extreme temperatures, air pollution, or allergens, sleep quality may be compromised rather than improved.

* [Indoor Air / Wiley Study on Bedroom Air Quality](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ina.12254)
* [Eindhoven University Research Portal](https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/windowdoor-opening-mediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on/)
* [PubMed: Sleep Quality Affected by Carbon Dioxide](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32979003/)
* [Technical University of Denmark: Bedroom Ventilation Research](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day)
